title: HTTP Over TLS
subtitle: Securing the web by layering HTTP over TLS, establishing the foundation for all secure web communication.
summary: RFC 2818 says how to run HTTP over TLS, which is what people call HTTPS. The client starts a TLS handshake on port 443 (TCP) before sending any HTTP, then sends ordinary HTTP as TLS application data. It also says the client must check that the server's certificate matches the host name in the URL, to stop man-in-the-middle attacks.

eli5.summary: Before you say anything private to a website, your computer and the website agree on a secret code, and your computer checks the website's name tag to be sure it is really talking to the right one.

questions: how does a browser check an https certificate
what is the difference between http and https

tldr.problem: HTTP sends everything in the clear, so anyone on the path can read or change it, and a client cannot tell whether it reached the real server.
tldr.mechanism: The client opens a TLS connection (default port 443), checks the server certificate against the host name in the URL, then sends normal HTTP requests as TLS application data.
tldr.outcome: Encryption plus server identity checking became the default for the web, and the https scheme is now the norm.

today: HTTPS is now the default way to use the web, and browsers warn on plain HTTP pages. The RFC Editor lists RFC 2818 as obsoleted by RFC 9110 (HTTP Semantics), which carries the HTTPS rules forward, and it was earlier updated by RFC 5785 and RFC 7230. The host name check in section 3.1 is still the core idea. Note that this document allows falling back to the Common Name, which major browsers no longer do: they require a subjectAltName.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP Over TLS (commonly known as HTTPS) provides a mechanism for securing HTTP connections using TLS (Transport Layer Security). This is the cornerstone of web security, enabling encrypted communication between browsers and servers.

HTTPS is simply HTTP layered on top of TLS/SSL. The protocol itself is not different from HTTP; it uses TLS to encrypt the entire HTTP conversation.

Default Port
HTTPS uses port 443 instead of HTTP's port 80
URI Scheme
URLs use the https:// scheme identifier
sections.eli5: Think of mailing a postcard versus a sealed letter. Plain HTTP is the postcard: anyone who handles it can read it. HTTPS puts the same message in a sealed envelope.

sections.title: Connection Initiation
sections.content:
The client initiates a TLS connection to the server on port 443. Once the TLS handshake is complete, the client sends its first HTTP request. All HTTP data is sent as TLS application data.

HTTP
HTTPS
Port 80
Port 443
Plaintext
Encrypted
http:// scheme
https:// scheme
sections.eli5: First your computer knocks on a special door (number 443) and sets up the secret code. Only after that does it ask for the web page, so the whole conversation is hidden.

sections.title: Endpoint Identification
sections.content:
The client must verify the server's identity using the certificate presented during the TLS handshake. The hostname in the URI must match the identity in the server's certificate.

If the hostname does not match the certificate, the client MUST either notify the user or terminate the connection. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks.

Certificate matching rules:

dNSNameMatch against the hostname using wildcard rules
iPAddressMatch against the host IP if connecting by IP
Common NameLegacy fallback if no dNSName subjectAltName is present
sections.eli5: Your computer reads the name tag on the website's certificate and checks that it says the same name as the address you typed. If the names do not match, it warns you or hangs up, because it might be talking to an impostor.

sections.title: Impact on the Modern Web
sections.content:
HTTPS has become the de facto standard for all web communication. Major browsers now flag HTTP sites as "Not Secure,".

Let's Encrypt
Free, automated certificates have made HTTPS much easier to deploy
HSTS
HTTP Strict Transport Security (RFC 6797) forces HTTPS-only connections
Mixed Content
Browsers block or warn about insecure resources loaded on HTTPS pages
sections.eli5: Nowadays almost every website uses the sealed envelope, and browsers fuss when one does not.

messages.note: The HTTP client also acts as the TLS client and starts the handshake.

messages.label: Certificate (and rest of handshake)
messages.note: The client checks the host name against this certificate (section 3.1).

messages.label: HTTP request as TLS application data
messages.note: Sent only after the TLS handshake has finished.

messages.label: HTTP response as TLS application data
TLS closure alert
messages.note: Both sides should exchange closure alerts before closing, so truncation can be detected.
